forecasts.question: Will OpenAI and Anthropic have a combined ARR exceeding $70B by 31 December 2026?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 99 to 99 (held).

Six triggers were live going into today. None fired cleanly, one fired weakly in the NO direction, and one piece of yesterday's own text needs correcting downwards. The net is zero, and I hold at 99 with the interval unchanged at [98, 99].

Trigger one, the public S-1. Still nothing. Anthropic's confidential draft S-1 went to the SEC on 1 June 2026 (Anthropic's own announcement and CNBC, 1 June), and reporting since July has had the public filing landing as early as late August, which would keep a Q4 Nasdaq listing on track. As at this morning the only S-1s on EDGAR this week are unrelated small caps such as Electra Therapeutics on 28 August and Aptevo on 21 August. The New York Times reported in late August that an eventual listing could value Anthropic at around $2 trillion, and Goldman Sachs, JPMorgan and Morgan Stanley are leading a deal expected to raise more than $60bn. So the filing is close but has not happened, and the single event most capable of moving this question remains ahead of me rather than behind me.

Trigger two, a month-on-month decline in either run rate. No such report. Trigger three, Q3 revenue below roughly $7.5bn for OpenAI or $15bn for Anthropic. No Q3 figures exist yet for either firm; the freshest hard numbers are still Q2, and I found nothing newer today. Trigger four, a resolver clarification on ARR convention. None. Trigger five, a compute-financing accident. Here there was movement, and on balance it cuts towards YES rather than away from it. Reuters on 14 August had Nvidia's OpenAI guarantee cut back to under $120bn covering only the first roughly five-gigawatt phase of the Ohio project, down from the $250bn the WSJ trailed in late July that knocked Nvidia down 5% on 28 July. Nvidia has since partnered with six financial institutions on compute financing platforms targeting over $500bn of third-party capital. That is risk being spread off a single balance sheet rather than a raise failing, which is the opposite of the accident my trigger describes. Trigger six, an upward confirmation above $120bn combined or above $70bn for Anthropic alone. Not confirmed, and this is where I have to mark my own homework.

Yesterday I wrote that independent trackers put Anthropic's August ARR near $70bn. Rechecking today, what I can actually substantiate is that Anthropic is projected to finish 2026 with a run rate between $70bn and $90bn, and separately that its investors expect a $100-120bn exit rate. Those are projections, not a dated August print. The last confirmed Anthropic figure remains above $65bn at end-July, told to investors and reported by Bloomberg, CNBC, Axios, TechCrunch and Fortune on 17-18 August, on preliminary Q2 revenue of $11.5-11.6bn against $4.73bn in Q1 and $787m a year earlier, with positive adjusted operating income. I am striking the tracker claim and reverting to the reported figure. That is a small NO-direction correction to my evidence base, not to my conclusion.

OpenAI's leg is unchanged and I re-verified it: run rate above $40bn, roughly doubled from $20bn at end-2025, reported by Bloomberg on 13-14 August, with Greg Brockman telling staff the monthly run rate grew more than 20% in July alone on coding, subscriptions and advertising. Q2 recognised revenue was $6.7bn against $5.7bn in Q1, with the operating loss widening to $12.3bn from $9.3bn. Losses are not revenue, and this question asks about revenue. TechCrunch on 20 August had OpenAI gaining on Anthropic among business users, which softens the "OpenAI is losing the enterprise" frame that SiliconANGLE ran on 18 August.

So the arithmetic is where it was. Reported exit run rates of $65bn plus $40bn give about $105bn against a $70bn bar, four months before measurement, on a series that has risen every month. The harshest defensible haircut, 30% off Anthropic for gross Bedrock and Vertex bookings against OpenAI's net Azure treatment, gives $85.5bn. Applying 30% to both legs, which nobody actually proposes, gives $73.5bn and still clears. The only NO path left is a resolver annualising stale Q2 recognised revenue, $73.2bn, and then stacking a net-basis cut on top, and Q4 data will not support the first half of that.

Net adjustment: about -0.2pp for retracting the near-$70bn tracker claim, about +0.2pp for the Nvidia financing being restructured and syndicated rather than failing. Central holds at 99, interval [98, 99].
forecasts.base_rate: The right reference class is persistence of an already-satisfied threshold, not attainment of a distant one. The bar is exceeded by roughly 50% on the dated record four months before measurement, on a monotonically rising series, with no identified mechanism capable of a one-third reversal. Public forecasting platforms resolve such questions YES in the high nineties, and instances of a large private technology company's reported annualised revenue falling more than 30% within two quarters, absent fraud or exogenous collapse, are essentially unrepresented. The residual risk is resolution mechanics rather than the world changing: every live convention clears today, at about $105bn on reported exit run rates, about $85.5bn after a 30% net-basis haircut on Anthropic alone, and $73.2bn on the most adversarial reading of stale Q2 recognised revenue annualised. A 98-99% persistence anchor against under 1pp for the compound-restatement branch gives 98.5-99.

factors_up.factor: Threshold already exceeded by roughly 50% on the dated record
factors_up.detail: Anthropic above $65bn annualised at end-July (Bloomberg, CNBC, Axios, TechCrunch, 17 Aug 2026) plus OpenAI above $40bn (Bloomberg, 13-14 Aug 2026) equals about $105bn against a $70bn bar. That is four months of headroom on a series that has risen every month since end-2025.

factors_up.factor: Anthropic's single leg is close to the entire combined bar
factors_up.detail: Anthropic is projected to exit 2026 between $70bn and $90bn on published trajectory work, and its investors reportedly expect $100-120bn. On either path Anthropic alone clears or nearly clears $70bn, so the question survives even if OpenAI's leg were struck out entirely.

factors_up.factor: OpenAI's current quarter is reaccelerating rather than stalling
factors_up.detail: The mid-August investor briefing had the overall run rate up 35% quarter to date and enterprise up 50% quarter to date, and Greg Brockman told staff the monthly run rate grew more than 20% in July alone. TechCrunch on 20 Aug reported OpenAI gaining on Anthropic among business users. The 18% sequential figure that drove the stall narrative describes Q2, not the current quarter.

factors_up.factor: The Nvidia financing risk has been syndicated rather than failing
factors_up.detail: Reuters on 14 August had Nvidia's OpenAI guarantee cut to under $120bn covering only the first five-gigawatt phase in Ohio, and Nvidia has since partnered with six financial institutions on platforms targeting over $500bn of third-party capital. That is risk being spread, not a raise collapsing, which weakens the main NO channel.

factors_up.factor: Anthropic is now generating positive adjusted operating income
factors_up.detail: The Q2 disclosure carried a first positive adjusted operating income alongside $11.5-11.6bn of revenue, and SemiAnalysis's IPO preview has quarterly operating profit above $1bn in Q3 with gross margin back to the mid-60s. A cash-generative Anthropic is far less exposed to a financing squeeze inside the window.

factors_down.factor: The gross-versus-net accounting dispute is quantified at 20-30%
factors_down.detail: Anthropic books Bedrock and Vertex consumption gross while OpenAI books Azure-mediated revenue net, and OpenAI CRO Denise Dresser's memo alleged an $8bn overstatement on a then-$30bn base. Applied at 30% to Anthropic alone the combined figure is $85.5bn, and at 30% to both legs $73.5bn. Firmer than a week ago, but still clearing.

factors_down.factor: I over-read the August tracker evidence yesterday
factors_down.detail: I wrote yesterday that trackers put Anthropic's August ARR near $70bn. What I can actually substantiate today is a projected $70-90bn year-end exit rate, not a dated August print. The last confirmed figure remains above $65bn at end-July, so my evidence base is marginally thinner than I recorded.

factors_down.factor: Deceleration is the consensus frame on both legs
factors_down.detail: The May-to-July move from roughly $47bn to $65bn is about 17.5% monthly against roughly 55% earlier in the year, and OpenAI's Q2 was 18% sequential with the operating loss widening to $12.3bn from $9.3bn. This is a growth-rate story rather than a level story, but a sharp enough deceleration would compress the cushion.

factors_down.factor: Residual resolution-mechanics ambiguity
factors_down.detail: A resolver annualising stale Q2 recognised revenue gets $73.2bn, only 4.6% above the bar, and stacking a net-basis haircut on that is the one remaining NO path. OpenAI is expected to list only in 2027, so its leg will rest on press-reported run rates rather than audited disclosure inside the window.

factors_down.factor: Compute commitments dwarf revenue and infrastructure spend is cooling
factors_down.detail: Combined commitments are put at roughly $1.1 trillion through 2030 against about $17bn of combined 2025 revenue, and Forrester's Charlie Dai reads infrastructure spending as peaking faster than expected, with the monthly increment down to $29bn from a $40bn average earlier in 2026. A funding accident remains the only plausible route to a demand shock before December.

key_uncertainties: Which ARR convention the resolver applies: exit-month annualised run rate at about $105bn on reported figures, a 20-30% net-basis haircut on Anthropic at roughly $85.5bn, or trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised at $73.2bn on stale Q2 data but far higher once Q4 data exists.

Whether Anthropic's public S-1, still absent from EDGAR as at 29 August despite reporting that it could land in late August, forces a gross-to-net reclassification larger than the 20-30% partner share implied by the Dresser memo.
Whether the deceleration visible on both legs steepens through Q4, and whether it reflects genuine demand saturation or simply the arithmetic of a much larger base.

Whether the roughly $1.1 trillion of combined compute commitments through 2030 produces a financing accident inside the window, given the July-to-August retreat from a $250bn Nvidia guarantee to under $120bn plus syndicated third-party capital.
Whether credible outlets publish specifically Q4 2026 figures for both firms, given OpenAI is expected to list only in 2027 and so will have no audited public disclosure before the measurement date.
update_triggers: Revise DOWN if Anthropic's public S-1 discloses audited revenue on a net basis more than 30% below the reported $65bn run rate, beyond the partner-share haircut implied by the Dresser memo.
Revise DOWN if any credible outlet reports either company's monthly run rate falling month on month for the first time, rather than merely decelerating.
Revise DOWN if Bloomberg, WSJ, FT or The Information put OpenAI's Q3 revenue below roughly $7.5bn or Anthropic's below roughly $15bn, signalling a genuine stall rather than a slower climb.
Revise DOWN if the resolver clarifies that ARR means trailing-quarter recognised revenue annualised AND that a Q2-dated or net-basis figure will be used.

Revise DOWN if a compute-financing accident becomes visible before 31 December, such as a failed raise above $10bn, an Oracle or neocloud contract default, or reported layoffs at either firm tied to weak demand.
Revise UP if the public S-1 confirms a run rate at or above $65bn on an audited basis, or any September or October report puts the combined run rate above $120bn or Anthropic alone above $70bn.

forecasts.question: Will UK average annual real GDP growth exceed 1.5% across the 2030s (2030-2039)?
forecasts.key_change:
Move: 35 to 35 (held).

Yesterday I cut a point because I decided I had been crediting denominator news as if it were numerator news. Today I have gone looking for something that would justify moving again and I have not found it. The week of 25 to 29 August 2026 has produced no first-order news about the 2030s, so I am holding at 35 and leaving the interval at 22 to 49.

Taking the triggers in order. The OBR trigger for the 28 October Budget has not fired; there is nothing new from Charlotte Street this week, and the position remains the one I set out on 26 August, that the underlying productivity assumption was cut from 1.3 to 1.0 per cent in November 2025 and left there in March 2026, with analysts expecting a further 0.1 to 0.2 point trim. That trigger simply waits for the event.

My second trigger asked for evidence that the pickup shows up in output rather than only in lower measured labour input. It has fired weakly in both directions. The Resolution Foundation's Macroeconomic Policy Outlook for Q3 2026 is the strongest thing anyone has written against my denominator objection. It reports output per hour growing 1.1 per cent a year over the two years to Q2 2026, against a fall of 0.7 per cent a year in the two years before and 0.7 per cent in the late 2010s, and it argues the recovery is broad based rather than a single sector or an AI boom, with the same workers doing the same jobs in the same sectors. That is a direct answer to the composition story. It is not, however, an answer to the measurement story, because the Foundation's improvement still comes from replacing Labour Force Survey hours with administrative tax data, and GDP is measured independently of hours. So I take the breadth point and decline the level point, as I did yesterday. Pulling the other way, the ONS productivity flash of 18 August 2026 had output per hour falling 0.8 per cent quarter on quarter in Q2 2026, worse than the 0.5 per cent fall expected, though still up 0.7 per cent on the year. The ONS first quarterly estimate on 13 August had real GDP up 0.4 per cent in Q2 after 0.6 per cent in Q1, and 1.2 per cent on the year, which is exactly the quarterly run rate I set as the neutral marker rather than above it. The Foundation also puts the level of output per hour around 5 per cent below the OBR's final pre-Covid path, worth about 150 billion pounds a year or 4,500 pounds a worker. Whether that gap is a catch-up opportunity for the 2030s or permanent scarring is the crux of this question, and nothing this week settled it.

The Bank of England trigger has not fired. The only new Bank output I can find is a working paper of 21 August 2026 by Ludovica Ambrosino, Jenny Chan and Silvana Tenreyro on productivity and inflation dynamics, which is about how a productivity shift moves supply and demand and therefore inflation, not about the level of UK potential. It is orthogonal to this question. What I did find, and had not been scoring, is Andrew Bailey's Cutlers' Feast speech in Sheffield in May 2026, "Can AI make Cutlery?". He puts UK potential supply growth at about 2.8 per cent a year over 1990 to 2006, with productivity contributing 2.4 points and labour supply 0.4, and at about 1.3 per cent over the roughly fifteen years since the financial crisis, with productivity contributing only 0.4 points and labour supply 0.8. That decomposition is quietly important for the 2030s. The already weak 1.3 per cent of the past fifteen years was two thirds labour supply, and the ONS 2024 based projections do not permit a repeat, since they have the working age population rising only from 44.3 million to 45.8 million by 2034 with deaths exceeding births from 2026. On Bailey's own arithmetic, clearing 1.5 per cent in the 2030s with 0.2 to 0.5 points of labour input requires productivity of 1.0 to 1.3 points, which is between two and three times the post crisis rate the Governor cites. That confirms the mid thirties rather than moving it, because my base rate already assumed the thinner labour contribution, but it is a cleaner statement of the arithmetic than anything I had.

The planning and investment trigger has fired mildly upward. The August 2026 comparison of independent forecasts to HM Treasury has the average at 1.1 per cent for 2026, up from 1.0 per cent in July, and 1.2 per cent for 2027. On data centres, a 300 million pound package underpinned by the National Wealth Fund will expand DataVita's site and fund a new one in the North Lanarkshire AI Growth Zone, contracted to CoreWeave on a fifteen year lease. That is real capital with a fifteen year horizon, which is the right sort of commitment for this window, but roughly a hundred jobs at two sites is not a macroeconomic event.

The two downside triggers have not fired. Migration has not settled below 150,000, and no new Bank or ONS work has confirmed the market sector rate near 0.7 per cent beyond the Piton and Cadamagnani post of 27 August that I already scored.

The one thing I am adding as a live consideration, with a caveat about my confidence in it, is the energy shock. NIESR's summer outlook cut growth to 0.9 per cent this year and 1.0 per cent next, sharply below the 1.4 and 1.3 per cent it published in February, with David Aikman saying the Middle East conflict has laid bare how exposed the UK remains to global energy shocks. Independent commentary in August points to Hormuz disruption and a shallow global recession in the second half of 2026. For a question about 2030 to 2039 this cuts both ways. A downturn that falls in 2026 and 2027 leaves more recovery inside the window, which helps YES, and it is the single largest reason my distribution has a fat right tail. Against that, an energy shock this severe suppresses exactly the business investment that has to happen in the late 2020s if the 2030s are to be capital deep, and EY's August outlook already has business investment flat next year rather than up 1.0 per cent. I score these as roughly offsetting.

Mechanically I am where I was. Market sector productivity of 0.7 to 1.1 per cent, whole economy composition allowance, 0.2 to 0.5 points of labour input, a decade mean near 1.3 per cent with a standard deviation around 0.5 points. That gives 34 to 36 and I stay at 35.
forecasts.base_rate: Seven of seven completed UK decades since the 1950s averaged above 1.5 per cent, but that class comes from a regime of rising participation, a rising working-age share and US catch-up, none of which operates in the 2030s. Decomposing instead is more honest. Andrew Bailey, Cutlers' Feast, May 2026, puts UK potential supply growth at 2.8 per cent a year over 1990 to 2006, with productivity 2.4 points and labour supply 0.4, and at 1.3 per cent over the fifteen years since the crisis, with productivity 0.4 and labour supply 0.8. ONS 2024-based projections leave the 2030s with 0.2 to 0.5 points of labour input, so productivity must supply 1.0 to 1.3 points. Institutional central cases cluster at 1.25 to 1.5, with NIESR trend 1.25, IMF potential 1.4, IFS 1.4, EY 1.5 from 2027 and the OBR fifty-year baseline near 1.5, putting the threshold in the upper half of the plausible range.

factors_up.factor: Institutional central cases sit just below the bar rather than far below it
factors_up.detail: The IFS expects annual real GDP growth to average 1.4 per cent from 2026 onwards, EY's August 2026 outlook has 0.9 per cent this year then 1.5 per cent from 2027, the OBR fifty-year baseline is around 1.5 per cent and the IMF's potential estimate 1.4 per cent. The August 2026 comparison of independent forecasts to HM Treasury has the average at 1.1 per cent for 2026, up from 1.0 per cent in July, and 1.2 per cent for 2027. A distribution centred near 1.4 with a half-point standard deviation clears 1.5 reasonably often.

factors_up.factor: Resolution Foundation finds the productivity pickup is broad based, not a single sector
factors_up.detail: The Macroeconomic Policy Outlook for Q3 2026 reports output per hour growing 1.1 per cent a year over the two years to Q2 2026, against a fall of 0.7 per cent a year in the two years before and 0.7 per cent in the late 2010s, and stresses the gains come from the same workers doing the same jobs in the same sectors. That defeats the composition explanation even if it does not defeat the hours-measurement explanation. A broad-based improvement is the kind that persists into a decade.

factors_up.factor: Bank of England staff endorse the AI channel and the UK's position in it
factors_up.detail: Piton and Cadamagnani, Bank Underground, 27 August 2026, find the contribution of IT and other information services to productivity growth is larger in the UK than in France, Germany or Italy, cite cross-country evidence putting UK AI adoption just behind the US, and conclude AI adoption may materially and persistently lift UK productivity growth. Bailey's May 2026 Sheffield speech engages seriously with the same possibility. This is the bearish institution writing the bullish paragraph.

factors_up.factor: The Brexit drag is largely complete before the window opens
factors_up.detail: The Bank's central estimate is that potential productivity will be around 3.25 per cent lower than otherwise by the end of 2028, with the effect weighing on growth during the transition to that level. On that timing the 2030s inherit a lower level rather than a continuing negative growth contribution. This is decade-specific and works in favour of YES.

factors_up.factor: A near-term downturn leaves recovery growth inside the window
factors_up.detail: NIESR's summer outlook cut growth to 0.9 per cent in 2026 and 1.0 per cent in 2027, from 1.4 and 1.3 per cent in February, citing the UK's exposure to global energy shocks after the Middle East conflict. If the cycle troughs in 2026 or 2027, the 2030s inherit an output gap to close rather than one to open. The Resolution Foundation's estimate that output per hour is around 5 per cent below the OBR's final pre-Covid path, worth roughly 150 billion pounds a year, is the size of the prize if any of it is cyclical.

factors_down.factor: Bailey's own decomposition shows the recent 1.3 per cent was mostly labour supply
factors_down.detail: At the Cutlers' Feast in May 2026 the Governor put post-crisis potential supply growth at about 1.3 per cent a year, with productivity contributing only 0.4 points and labour supply 0.8, against 2.4 and 0.4 respectively over 1990 to 2006. The 2030s cannot repeat a 0.8 point labour contribution. Clearing 1.5 per cent therefore requires productivity of 1.0 to 1.3 points, between two and three times the rate the Bank attributes to the past fifteen years.

factors_down.factor: The Bank's market-sector numbers are well below the bar
factors_down.detail: Bank Underground, 27 August 2026, has UK market-sector output per hour growing 0.3 per cent a year over 2008-19 and 0.7 per cent over 2020 to 2025 Q3, against 2.5 per cent over 1998-2007 and US rates of 1.5 and 2.2. Adding 0.2 to 0.5 points of labour input to 0.7 per cent leaves a decade mean near 1.0. The ONS flash of 18 August 2026 then had output per hour falling 0.8 per cent in Q2 2026, worse than the 0.5 per cent expected.

factors_down.factor: Much of the productivity good news is denominator, not numerator
factors_down.detail: ESCoE work cited by the Bank suggests the ONS move to component-based hours would lift measured 2008-19 productivity growth by around 0.4 points, and the LSE tax-record work has employment down 133,000 where the official series shows a rise of 377,000. GDP is measured independently of hours, so these re-split a given output number rather than adding to it. The Resolution Foundation's 1.1 per cent likewise rests on swapping the Labour Force Survey denominator for administrative data.

factors_down.factor: Demographics cap labour input at 0.2 to 0.5 points a year
factors_down.detail: ONS 2024-based projections have the population rising from 69.3 million in mid-2024 to 71.0 million by 2034 with all growth from net migration, and the working-age population rising only from 44.3 million to 45.8 million, with deaths exceeding births from 2026. Net migration was 171,000 in the year to December 2025, below the 230,000 long-run assumption from 2028, and immigration policy continues to tighten under the May 2025 white paper reforms.

factors_down.factor: Investment weak, capital deepening thin, and an energy shock on top
factors_down.detail: EY's August 2026 outlook has business investment flat next year, revised down from plus 1.0 per cent, and ONS provisional Q2 2026 business investment sits only 0.8 per cent above a year earlier. The Bank notes the UK business investment-to-GDP ratio has been below other G7 economies since the turn of the century. A severe energy shock in 2026 suppresses exactly the late-2020s investment that has to happen for the 2030s to be capital deep.

key_uncertainties: Whether the 5 per cent shortfall of output per hour against the OBR's final pre-Covid path, which the Resolution Foundation values at roughly 150 billion pounds a year or 4,500 pounds a worker, is a catch-up opportunity for the 2030s or permanent scarring. Nothing published this week distinguishes the two.

Which productivity series is right. Estimates for the same economy span 0.7 per cent on the Bank's market-sector measure to 1.8 per cent on Morgan Stanley's private-sector estimate. Because GDP is measured independently of hours, part of that dispersion is informative about future output and part is an argument about the denominator that leaves GDP growth untouched.

Whether the AI contribution scales beyond IT and information services. The Bank's evidence is a tenth of a point from software and IT consulting and a favourable UK position in J62-63. Whether diffusion reaches health, social care, construction and public services is the single largest swing factor in this forecast.

Whether the Middle East energy shock troughs before 2030 or leaves a persistent investment scar. NIESR cut 2026 and 2027 to 0.9 and 1.0 per cent on this account. A trough outside the window helps YES, a suppressed late-2020s capital stock hurts it, and I currently score these as offsetting.

Whether net migration settles near the ONS long-run assumption of about 230,000 a year from 2028 or nearer the 171,000 recorded for the year to December 2025. The gap is worth roughly 0.2 points a year on headline GDP growth, a large fraction of the distance to the threshold.
update_triggers: Revise UP if the OBR at the 28 October 2026 Budget EFO raises, or explicitly declines to cut, its 1.0 per cent underlying productivity assumption and cites the administrative-data evidence, or moves its medium-term path back toward 1.1 to 1.3 per cent; that would be worth 5 to 8 points.

Revise UP if the ONS quarterly national accounts on 30 September 2026 or the Q3 productivity release on 17 November 2026 pair stronger output per hour with stable or rising hours, or if Q3 GDP comes in above the 0.4 per cent quarterly run rate recorded for Q2 2026.

Revise UP if the Bank of England extends the Piton and Cadamagnani AI-productivity finding beyond IT and information services into large-employment sectors, or raises its potential supply estimate above the 1.3 per cent Bailey cited in May 2026 in the 5 November 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

Revise UP if the August 2026 NPPF and the critical national infrastructure designation for data centres produce a measurable acceleration in major consents, or if the CBI Industrial Trends and EY investment intentions for 2027 turn clearly positive after EY's downgrade to flat.

Revise DOWN if the OBR cuts its trend productivity assumption again on 28 October by the 0.1 to 0.2 points analysts expect, if the Budget package is scored as net contractionary for potential output, or if public capital spending is cut to restore headroom.

Revise DOWN if net migration settles durably below 150,000 a year, if the ONS revises working-age population growth to 2034 below 0.3 per cent a year, or if the energy shock persists such that NIESR or the OBR cut UK trend growth rather than only the 2026 and 2027 cyclical path.
